lesson.title: Pairing Up: What Makes a Relation
lesson.summary: A relation is simply any set of ordered pairs connecting input values to output values, the raw material that functions are built from.
lesson.body:
Before you can understand what a function is, you need to understand the broader category it belongs to: a relation. A relation is any set of ordered pairs, where each pair connects one value to another. That is the entire definition, nothing more is required. If you have a list of points like (1, 2), (3, 4), and (5, 6), that list is a relation, because it associates each first number with a second number. Relations show up constantly in everyday life: a list pairing each student's name with a test score, a table pairing each day of the week with a high temperature, or a graph pairing each x-coordinate with a y-coordinate are all relations.

The two numbers in each ordered pair usually come from two related sets. The set of all first coordinates is called the domain of the relation, and the set of all second coordinates is called the range. This is the same idea you use when plugging a number in for a variable: the variable represents a placeholder, and a relation is what happens once you start filling that placeholder with actual paired values. A relation can be written several different ways: as a list of ordered pairs, as a table with two rows or columns, as a graph of points on a coordinate plane, as a mapping diagram with arrows, or as an equation connecting two variables.

Consider the relation given by the ordered pairs (-1, 3), (0, 5), (2, 5), and (4, 9). This is a perfectly valid relation. Its domain, the set of first coordinates, is -1, 0, 2, and 4. Its range, the set of second coordinates, is 3, 5, and 9, listing the repeated value 5 only once. Notice something here: the input 0 and the input 2 both produce the same output, 5. Relations are perfectly comfortable with repeated outputs, and they are even comfortable with repeated inputs pointing to different outputs, such as adding the pair (0, 8) to the list above, where the input 0 would now map to both 5 and 8.

That last observation matters a great deal, because it is exactly the dividing line between a general relation and the more restrictive, more useful category called a function. Not every relation is a function, but every function is a relation, the same way every square is a rectangle but not every rectangle is a square. Relations are the wide, permissive category, and functions are the well-behaved subset where each input is only allowed to connect to exactly one output.

Understanding relations first, before functions, mirrors how you first learned to work with a single variable before working with two variables at once. A relation is what happens when a variable's value is paired with another variable's value, and studying that pairing, in every form it can take, is the groundwork for everything else in this unit: domain, range, function notation, and evaluating functions all start from this simple idea of ordered pairs connecting one set of values to another.
